Nodes 1, 3, and 5 form the dominating set (accent); an accent edge links each other node to a set member that dominates it. The card shows the result [1, 3, 5], size 3." width="100%"} A dominating set `D` of a graph `G = (V, E)` is a subset of V such that every vertex not in `D` is adjacent to at least one member of `D`. This method uses a greedy algorithm that finds some dominating set, but not necessarily the minimum one. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [start_with]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional node ID to start the algorithm from. If `None`, the smallest node ID is used. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of node IDs forming a dominating set. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the `start_with=` node doesn't exist in the graph. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} A simple greedy sweep in $O(V + E)$ that starts from `start_with=` (or the smallest node ID if unset), repeatedly adds the smallest-ID unmarked node, and marks it and its neighbors as dominated until every node is covered. The result is deterministic for a given graph. The result is *some* dominating set but not the smallest one possible; the minimum dominating set problem is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard, so this heuristic mainly earns its keep as a fast baseline. Any maximal independent set is automatically a dominating set, since every excluded vertex must be adjacent to an included one, so `maximal_independent_set()` provides another cheap route to the same guarantee. For a weighted objective, `min_weighted_dominating_set()` is preferable. ## Examples {.doc-examples} On a random graph, the greedy algorithm produces some dominating set (not necessarily the smallest possible), which can be verified with `is_dominating_set()`: ::: {#6eb6b04a .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_gnm_graph(n=100, m=200, seed=23) dom = graph.dominating_set() # Returns True: every node is either in the set or adjacent to a member graph.is_dominating_set(dom) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` True ``` ::: ::: In a star graph, the hub alone dominates every leaf, so starting the search there gives the smallest possible dominating set right away: ::: {#5ebad5b4 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_star_graph(10) # Hub with 9 leaves dom = graph.dominating_set(start_with=1) # Start from the hub # Returns 1 (just the hub) len(dom) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 1 ``` ::: ::: Every maximal independent set is also a dominating set (since any node not in the set must be adjacent to one that is), so the two methods often produce comparably-sized results: ::: {#2b1523f7 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_cycle_graph(8) dom = graph.dominating_set() ind = graph.maximal_independent_set(seed=23) # Compare the two set sizes (len(dom), len(ind)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (4, 3) ``` ::: :::
